title: Checkpoint: Weighing Evidence
objective: After this level you can rank evidence from weak to strong and explain what makes the difference.
summary: Carl Sagan's 1995 baloney detection kit, read as a map of the chapter: independent confirmation, the traps of ignorance, small numbers and selected evidence, and a warning about misuse.

cards.headline: In 1995, Carl Sagan packed a toolkit for testing claims.
cards.body: He called it a baloney detection kit, and it fills a chapter of his book The Demon-Haunted World. Remember Sagan's slogan from Level 38? His kit reads like a map of this whole chapter. Let's open it.

cards.headline: The first tool
cards.body: The kit starts with things to do, and the first is: wherever possible, there must be independent confirmation of the "facts". That's Level 39's cable. One vivid story or one witness is a single fiber. Before you rank a claim as well supported, look for a second line of evidence that could have failed on its own.

cards.headline: Traps in the kit, and where you met them

items.label: Appeal to ignorance
points: Not proved false, so true, or the reverse

items.label: Statistics of small numbers
points: Too few cases for the conclusion

items.label: Observational selection
points: Counting the hits and forgetting the misses

cards.headline: Handle with care
cards.body: Sagan added a warning: like all tools, the kit can be misused, applied out of context, or used as a rote substitute for thinking. Spotting a trap tells you the evidence is weak, not that the claim is false. Weigh what's there, then decide how sure to be.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: How to rank evidence, from a lone story up to independent lines that agree.
Why the one making a claim must back it, and when "not found" really counts.
Which traps skew evidence: small or unusual samples, picked cases and missing survivors.
Why a surprising claim needs stronger evidence without being ruled out.

questions.prompt: What is the first tool in Carl Sagan's baloney detection kit?

options.label: Trust the most confident speaker
options.rationale: Confidence isn't one of Sagan's tools.

options.label: Seek independent confirmation of the facts
Reject any claim that sounds surprising
options.rationale: Surprising claims need more evidence, not automatic rejection.

options.label: Count only the cases that fit
options.rationale: That's a trap in the kit, not a tool.

questions.explanation: The kit's first tool: wherever possible, there must be independent confirmation of the "facts".

questions.prompt: Sagan's kit warns against "counting the hits and forgetting the misses". How does that trap mislead?

options.label: It uses a sample that's far too large
options.rationale: The problem is which cases, not how many.

options.label: It shifts the burden of proof onto the listener
It shows only the cases that fit the claim
It treats a lack of evidence as proof

questions.explanation: Keeping the hits and dropping the misses shows only the helpful evidence, the same move as cherry-picking.

questions.prompt: Weighing Evidence checkpoint: in a U.S. criminal trial, which side carries the burden of proof?

options.label: The defense, which must prove innocence
The judge, who must find the truth
options.rationale: The judge doesn't carry the burden.

options.label: Whichever side speaks first
The prosecution, which must prove guilt

questions.explanation: The prosecution carries the burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; the defendant is presumed innocent.

questions.prompt: Famous rich dropouts make a degree look pointless. Which error is at work?

options.label: Survivorship bias
Appeal to ignorance
options.rationale: Nobody is treating missing evidence as proof.

options.label: Misplaced burden of proof
Consilience
options.rationale: Consilience is independent evidence agreeing, a strength.

questions.explanation: You hear about the dropouts who got rich, not the great majority who didn't: attention only to what passed a filter.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest evidence that a new bike lock resists thieves?

options.label: A friend's story that his was never stolen
options.rationale: One story is one case: an anecdote.

options.label: Nobody has proved it can be broken
options.rationale: Without a real test, that's an appeal to ignorance.

options.label: Several independent tests that agree
One impressive test run by the maker
options.rationale: A single line of evidence, from an interested source.

questions.explanation: Independent lines that agree form a cable: each could have failed on its own, and none did.
